normalized.governing_thought: Fix promotions, shrink and delivery pricing, rebalance labor and exit loss-making stores: margin returns to ~2.9–3.1% by FY2028. The 8% labor cut should not go ahead.
executive_summary: Diagnosis: Gross margin and e-commerce delivery explain ~80% of the 2.4-point margin decline. Wages explain 13%.
More promotions (24%→29% of sales) and higher shrink (2.1%→2.6%) fully explain the gross-margin loss. 38% of FY2025 promotion events lost money.
E-commerce loses ~$10M a year once third-party delivery and cannibalisation are counted. The team reports a 6.1% profit.
Plan: Eight actions add ~$29M of operating income. After the 2027 wage step, FY2028 operating income is ~$41M (2.9%).
Gross margin +$16.3M (promotions, vendor funding, private label, shrink). Labor rebalance +$3.6M. Delivery pricing +$2.5M. Exiting nine stores +$6.6M.
Taking shrink back to FY2023's 2.1% closes the gap to the 3.0% target (3.1%). One-time cost is ~$20M, inside the $25M cap.
First moves: Four fast, low-cost moves start this quarter. Within ~6 months they lift run-rate operating income to ~$26M, above the $20M covenant.
Roll out the tested delivery fee. Drop loss-making promotions. Rebalance labor hours instead of cutting 8%. Give notice on the six leases that expire.
The 8% cut saves $14.5M on paper. If shrink responds as it did in FY2023–25, ~$10M of that comes back as shrink, and fresh produce (the top reason to shop at Harlow) suffers.
Risks: Even in the low case, FY2028 operating income is ~$27M (2.0%). ValuMart's response and vendor funding are the largest uncertainties.
Stage gates in Q2 and Q4 FY2027. Contingency levers if we fall behind: shrink stretch, delivery contract re-tender, a further targeted hours trim.
Board decisions: approve the plan and budget, withdraw the blanket cut, vote on three store exits, and confirm 'delivery in some form' with the owners.

slides.title: We started from the hypothesis that commercial fixes alone would be enough. They reach only ~2.1%, so labor rebalancing and store exits are also needed.

claims.claim: Initial answer: The decline is commercial, not wage-driven. Fix promotions and e-commerce pricing; avoid labor cuts and store closures.
Revised answer: Commercial fixes lead, but labor must be rebalanced and the nine loss-making stores exited to reach ~2.9–3.1%.
1. Wages are not the main cause — Holds
evidence: Store labor's share of the 2.36-pt margin decline: 0.30 pt = 13% of the decline

claims.claim: 2. The gross-margin loss is controllable (mix and shrink, not cost of goods) — Holds
3. E-commerce destroys value and pricing can fix it — Partly: contain, don't grow
evidence: −$10.4M a year; tested pricing recovers $2.5M, leaving −$7.6M

claims.claim: 4. Store hours cannot be cut safely — Partly: no blanket cut; a targeted trim is safe
evidence: Shrink Q1 3.1% vs Q4 2.3%, but Q3 ≈ Q4 (2.4% vs 2.3%)

claims.claim: 5. Commercial + e-commerce levers alone reach 3.0% — Fails: add labor rebalance and store exits

slides.title: Operating margin fell 2.4 points in two years. Gross margin and e-commerce fulfillment drove ~80% of the fall; store labor drove 13%.

claims.claim: Operating margin bridge FY2023→FY2025: 3.37% → 1.02%
Sales grew $83M (+5.8%), yet operating income fell $32.6M, from $47.9M to $15.3M.
Management's diagnosis (wages) covers only 13% of the fall. A plan built around labor cannot reach 3.0%.
The two big drivers are commercial choices: promotional intensity and how delivery is priced.

slides.title: Wages rose 9.4%, but fewer hours per $ of sales absorbed most of it. The thinner staffing now shows up as shrink.

claims.claim: Wages rose 9.4%, but fewer hours per $ of sales absorbed most of it.
evidence: Wage effect at FY2023 hours: +1.11 pt (≈ $16.7M)
Net ≈ +0.34 pt, matches reported +0.3 pt within rounding (≈ $4.5M)

claims.claim: Shrink rose 0.5 pt (≈ $7.5M), more than the $4.5M net rise in labor cost. Further across-the-board cuts would repeat the trade that is already hurting margin.
The lowest-labor quartile runs 0.8 pt more shrink than the highest. Its managers say produce rotation and receiving checks are skipped on busy days.
evidence: Shrink by labor-intensity quartile FY2025: Q1 (fewest hours) 3.1%, Q2 2.7%, Q3 2.4%, Q4 (most hours) 2.3%

claims.claim: Q3 and Q4 differ by only 0.1 pt, so hours in the most labor-intensive stores can be trimmed with little shrink risk.
Mix of shrink: produce and fresh waste 45%, theft 35%, admin and receiving errors 20%.

slides.title: Heavier promotions and rising shrink fully explain the gross-margin loss. The extra promotions did not make customers see Harlow as better value.

claims.claim: Gross-margin bridge FY2023→FY2025: 26.04% → 25.02%; the three drivers sum to −1.02 pt, exactly the reported fall.
38% of FY2025 promotion events lost money even after counting the extra units they sold.
Vendor funding fell from 55% to 46% of promotional markdowns, so Harlow pays for more of each event.
Price perception got worse: 41% of shoppers now call Harlow 'more expensive', up from 33%.
The category team's comp claim does not prove promotions pay; comps are not profit, and the comparison is not controlled for location.
evidence: 1.6 pt of extra sales at 20¢ contribution is worth 0.32% of sales
pays only if those stores carry less than 2.3 pt of extra promotion share (0.32 ÷ 0.14)

claims.claim: Shrink is $39M a year (2.6% of sales). Every 0.1 pt is worth ~$1.5M.
Private label is the one positive: each extra point of share adds ~$1.8M of gross profit.

slides.title: Counting third-party delivery and cannibalised store sales, e-commerce loses ~$10M a year. Each home delivery loses ~$12.

claims.claim: True annual contribution of e-commerce FY2025 is −$10.4M
Each home delivery loses ~$12.
evidence: Contribution per order ($96 × 30% new × 20¢) $5.76 collect / $5.76 delivered

claims.claim: Why the team's '6.1% profit' is wrong: it leaves out third-party delivery, which costs $8.3M net of fees and is booked in 'E-commerce fulfillment'.
It counts every online sale as new to Harlow. Customers say 70% would otherwise have been bought in a Harlow store.
Growth made the loss bigger.
evidence: Net fulfillment cost rose from $5.2M to $18.1M as orders tripled and home delivery's share rose from 45% to 58%

slides.title: Eight actions add ~$29M a year. After the 2027 wage step, FY2028 operating income reaches ~$41M (2.9%). A shrink stretch closes the gap to 3.0%.

claims.claim: Operating income bridge FY2025 → FY2028 base case: $15.3M → $40.7M
Every action maps to one P&L line; Other SG&A has stayed flat at 4.7% of sales, so the plan has no lever there.
Base case = 2.9% (40.7 ÷ 1,398). Stretch: shrink back to FY2023's 2.1% adds $2.8M → $43.5M = 3.1%.
Store exits lower sales by $88.5M (the 75% not transferred), which lifts the margin ratio.
Wage step: +4% minimum wage = $7.3M; we assume half is recovered in pricing.

slides.title: Four gross-margin actions add ~$16M. The largest is dropping the promotion events that already lose money.

claims.claim: Promotions: cut the loss-making events first; promotion share back toward FY2023: +5.1
evidence: 4 pt × 14 pt margin gap × $1,412M = $7.9M; less 1% volume loss ($14.1M × 20¢ = $2.8M)

claims.claim: Vendor funding: make funding a condition of promotion slots: +3.6
evidence: Markdowns ≈ 14 pt ÷ (1 − 46%) = 25.9% of promoted sales; 25% × $1,398M × 25.9% = $90.6M × 4 pt

claims.claim: Private label: extend range in fresh and staples: +3.4
evidence: 2 pt × 12 pt margin gap × $1,398M; trend was +0.75 pt a year in FY2023–25

claims.claim: Shrink: produce rotation, receiving checks, loss prevention: +4.2
evidence: 0.3 pt × $1,398M; Q3–Q4 stores already run 2.3–2.4%. Stretch 2.1% (FY2023) adds +$2.8M

claims.claim: Total gross-margin actions +16.3

Cutting promotions risks traffic in the stores that compete with ValuMart. Mitigation: cut the loss-making events first, and if needed reinvest up to $2M in everyday prices on key items in those stores.
The vendor-funding value depends on how markdowns are recorded, and the pack does not say. We read the 14-pt gap as net of funding.
evidence: Each point of funding is ~$0.9M; full recovery to 55% would be ~$8M

slides.title: Rolling out the tested delivery pricing saves ~$2.5M a year and keeps home delivery. The service still loses money, so growth stays frozen.

claims.claim: Fee test applied to FY2025 volumes yields net gain of +2.5 to +2.8 $M a year (plan uses $2.5M)
evidence: Contribution lost on 2% lower sales +0.2 to +0.5

claims.claim: Delivery contract renews in 2026. The provider wants +3%, which costs $0.3M. Re-tender instead: each 5% off the rate is worth ~$0.5M.
Keep growth frozen until both order types make money.
evidence: Click-and-collect breaks even at 38.5% new-to-Harlow sales (we have 30%), or at a picking cost of $5.76

claims.claim: Options considered: grow e-commerce as is rejected; exit home delivery kept only as fallback; further pricing steps to be tested.
evidence: Home delivery still loses ~$9 per order after repricing (~$6M a year)

claims.claim: Caveat: the test ran in 4 stores for 10 weeks. Roll out in waves and stop if e-commerce sales fall more than 5%.

slides.title: A targeted labor rebalance nets ~$3.6M with little risk. The 8% blanket cut could give back most of its $14.5M through shrink and lost sales.

claims.claim: Management draft (8% of hours in every store) nets +1.5 to +14.5, central ~+4.5 before any sales loss
evidence: Shrink effect up to −10.0 if shrink responds as in FY2023–25 (−6% hours ↔ +0.5 pt) → +0.67 pt
Sales at risk: each 1% of sales lost = −3.0

claims.claim: Recommended targeted rebalance nets +3.6
evidence: Gross saving +5.5 (~5% of hours in the most labor-intensive half of stores ≈ 3% of chain hours)
Reinvestment −1.8 (1% of chain hours put back into produce rotation and receiving in the lowest-labor stores)
Shrink effect neutral to positive: Q3 and Q4 stores differ by 0.1 pt of shrink
Sales at risk low: fresh and receiving hours are protected

claims.claim: Cutting labor while ValuMart competes on price leaves Harlow with neither advantage.
evidence: Top reasons to shop at Harlow: fresh produce (58%) and convenience (44%)

claims.claim: Trim hours in Q3–Q4 stores toward the Q3 level, protect task standards; reverse in any store where shrink rises more than 0.2 pt.
The 2027 minimum-wage rise (+4%) adds ~$7.3M; plan assumes half recovered in prices (−$3.6M net). If none is recovered, contingency is a further 1% targeted hours trim (+$1.8M).

slides.title: Exiting the nine stores with negative four-wall EBITDA adds ~$6.6M a year. Six can close when their leases expire, with no lease-exit cost.

claims.claim: Exiting all nine stores adds +6.6 $M a year
evidence: Governance: management decision; board vote required

claims.claim: Do not renew the six expiring leases. Run a store-by-store review of the other three and bring them to a board vote in Q2 FY2027.
Without the three that need a board vote, FY2028 margin is ~2.7%, and $8.7M of one-time cost is avoided.
The pack gives totals only; the real split may differ, so the store review must confirm each case.
evidence: $0.4M per store non-lease closure cost is a planning assumption

slides.title: Of the options assessed, only the recommended plan gets close to 3.0% within the capital cap and the owners' commitments.

evidence: Main risk: Shrink and service; treats a minor cause
$15.3M + $14.5M − $3.6M = $26.2M at best; with shrink response (−$10M) and 1% lost sales (−$3M), $13.2M

claims.claim: B. Recommended: all eight actions — within $25M; board vote on 3 stores
evidence: Main risk: traffic response to fewer promotions; vendor funding

claims.claim: C. B without the three board-vote store exits — no board vote needed
D. B plus exit home delivery — breaks the owners' delivery commitment
evidence: adds ~$6.4M that repriced home delivery still loses (703k orders × $9.04), less some contribution from switching customers

claims.claim: E. Grow e-commerce as is — fits

slides.title: Start with four moves that are proven, cheap and quick. Slower, larger levers follow once they are under way.

claims.claim: Wave 1 (now): four moves
evidence: 1. Roll out tested delivery pricing; re-tender delivery contract: +2.5; one-time 0.5; 1–3 months; High: in-market test
2. Drop loss-making promotion events (share 29%→25%): +5.1; 1.0; 3–6 months; High: post-event review
3. Rebalance labor hours, with fresh and receiving standards: +3.6; 1.5; 3–6 months; Medium: shrink-by-quartile data
4. Give notice on the six expiring leases: +4.4; 2.4; at lease end (by end-2027); High: four-wall P&L

claims.claim: Waves 2–3 follow
evidence: 5. Recover vendor funding (46%→50%): +3.6; incl. in 2; 6–12 months; Low–medium; Wave 2 FY2027
6. Shrink program to 2.3% (stretch 2.1%): +4.2; 4.0; 6–18 months; Medium; Wave 2 FY2027
7. Extend private-label range (18.5%→20.5%): +3.4; 2.0; 12–24 months; Medium; Wave 2 FY2027–28
8. Exit three stores with leases beyond 2027: +2.2; 8.7; FY2028; Medium: totals only; Wave 3 after board vote

claims.claim: Wave 1 holds the actions with the highest value per dollar and per month of delay, backed by Harlow's own test or review data, and they are reversible. Action 4's decision cannot wait: missing a notice date locks in a loss-making store.

slides.title: Wave 1 lifts run-rate operating income to ~$26M within six months, clear of the $20M covenant. Two stage gates keep the plan honest.

~$28M FY2027 (net of wage step), ≈1.9%; partial-year effects

evidence: Promotions 3.5 / 5.1 / 8.0 (traffic loss when events are cut)

slides.title: Each major risk has an early signal and a pre-agreed response. If the plan falls behind, the contingency levers are worth ~$5M.

claims.claim: ValuMart takes traffic as promotions are cut
evidence: Signal: comps and basket count in stores within 3 miles of ValuMart vs the rest
Response: cut loss-making events first; up to $2M for everyday prices on key items

claims.claim: Vendors do not restore funding
evidence: Signal: funding as % of markdowns, by supplier
Response: tie promotion slots to funding; move events to suppliers that fund

claims.claim: Delivery customers leave faster than in the test
evidence: Signal: weekly delivered orders; e-commerce sales vs −2%
Response: roll out in waves; pause if e-commerce sales fall more than 5%

claims.claim: Labor rebalance hurts shrink or service
evidence: Signal: shrink by quartile, checkout waits, out-of-stocks
Response: protect fresh and receiving hours; reverse where shrink rises more than 0.2 pt

claims.claim: Closed stores transfer less than 25% of sales
evidence: Signal: sales in the receiving stores
Response: retain customers (loyalty offers, click-and-collect from the receiving store)

claims.claim: Wage step not recovered in prices
Contingency released at Gate 2 if more than $3M behind, together ~$5M: enough to cover either vendor funding failing entirely or the wage step going wholly unrecovered, but not both.
evidence: further 1% targeted hours trim in Q4 stores (+$1.8M)
delivery contract re-tender beyond flat (+$0.5M per 5%)
vendor funding failing (−$3.6M); wage step unrecovered (−$3.6M)

normalized.extraction_notes: The deck was provided as plain text with no images.
